text: Read the sentence on the screen: the cat sat down because it was tired. You knew at once that it means the cat. A model that has only embeddings cannot know that, because the embedding of the word it is the same row of the table in every sentence ever written. To understand it here, the vector for it has to borrow information from the other words around it, and the question of this lesson is how a model decides which words to borrow from.

The idea is called attention, and it works like a good meeting. Each person updates their view by listening to everyone in the room, but they listen more closely to the people whose remarks are relevant to them. In the same way, every token builds a new vector as a blend of all the token vectors in the sentence, and a set of weights decides how much each one contributes. For the word it, we would like most of the weight to land on cat, and only a little on words like the or down.

Where do the weights come from? The simplest answer uses a tool you already have, the dot product. We take the vector for it and compute its dot product with every vector in the sentence, including its own. Vectors that point in similar directions give large scores, and unrelated ones give scores near zero or below. The result is one score per token, a row of raw numbers that says how strongly it relates to each word.

Raw scores are not yet weights, because they can be negative and they do not add up to anything in particular. So we pass them through a function called softmax, which exponentiates every score, making it positive, and then divides by the total, so the weights sum to one. Large scores win most of the weight, and small ones fade, though never quite to zero. We will look at softmax closely in a later lesson; for now, think of it as turning scores into shares of a whole.

With the weights in hand, the new vector for it is a weighted average: each token's vector is scaled by its weight, and the scaled vectors are added up. It is like mixing paint, where a large share of cat and a little of everything else gives a colour that is mostly cat. The output has the same length as the input vector, so it can take the original's place, but now it carries context from the rest of the sentence.

Now do this for every token at once, and the whole computation becomes two matrix products. Stack the token vectors into the matrix X, with one row per token. Multiplying X by its own transpose gives a square table of scores, one row for each token doing the looking, and one column for each token being looked at. Softmax is applied to each row separately, turning the table into attention weights, where every row sums to one. Multiplying the weights by X then produces every blended vector in a single step, and the output has the same shape as X.

This raw version has a flaw you can see in the table. The largest score in each row usually sits on the diagonal, because every vector is most similar to itself, so each token mostly looks at itself. Worse, the only reason to attend is plain similarity, while the word it should go looking for a noun, which is not at all the same thing as a word that resembles it. What is missing is a way to separate what a token is looking for from what it offers to others.

Even so, notice what we have gained. There is no chain and no index card: every token reaches every other token in one step, and the whole sentence is processed in parallel with two matrix multiplications. In the next lesson, we give each token three separate roles, called queries, keys and values, and attention becomes something a network can learn.
